title: GP2F: Dual-Branch Graph Prompting
one_liner: Keep the old graph-reading model frozen and train a lightweight adapter alongside it, then blend both using a loss that rewards agreement and respects the graph structure.
lead: When a graph-reading model (a neural network trained on one type of graph) sees a very different kind of graph in the real world, it often stumbles. This paper shows that the best approach is not to choose between staying frozen (keeping the old knowledge) or adapting fully (learning everything new), but to run both in parallel and let them vote together through careful alignment.

paras: A graph neural network is a model that reads graphs—networks where nodes (things) are connected by edges (relationships). Researchers pre-train these models on big graphs like social networks or protein interactions, learning general patterns about how nodes connect and what information flows. But when you try to use that model on a completely different type of graph—say, a tiny graph from a new domain with only a few labeled examples—the old patterns often mismatch. The model was trained to see one kind of graph structure; now it sees a different shape.

A beginner would try one of two things: freeze the old model entirely and just add a simple new layer on top (linear probing), or unfreeze everything and retrain the whole model on the new data (full fine-tuning). The frozen approach loses the chance to adapt. The unfrozen approach risks overwriting all the useful old knowledge with noise from a tiny dataset. Either way, something is wasted.

callout.html: Train two branches in parallel—one frozen, one adapted—and blend them using losses that make them agree and respect the graph structure.

steps.text: The pre-trained graph encoder stays locked; its weights never change.
Small trainable modules (adapters) wrap each layer of a copied encoder, updating only themselves.
A loss pulls the two branches' predictions for the same node closer together, rewarding agreement.
A second loss ensures the fused predictions respect the graph edges—nearby nodes should predict similarly.
Final prediction blends frozen and adapted representations, then feeds to a classifier.

paras: The paper introduces a second learnable branch (adapters) running parallel to the frozen encoder, instead of choosing one or the other. This dual structure lets the model hold both old knowledge and new learning at the same time.

hidden.name: Alignment between frozen and adapted predictions
paras: The paper measures how closely the two branches agree on what each node represents. If both the frozen (old-knowledge) and adapted (new-learning) branches produce the same high-level understanding of a node's role, they are well-aligned. This alignment is invisible in a single-branch model but critical here.

The paper estimates alignment using a contrastive loss: it computes how different the two branches' representations are, then penalizes large differences. When branches agree, the loss is small; when they disagree, the loss is large, so training tightens their alignment.

heat.caption: Darker means both branches predict the same class for that node.

reads.html: The two branches are allies when they agree. If frozen says node 5 is important and adapted says node 5 is important, that agreement is a signal that the answer is trustworthy.

The contrastive loss aligns representations by minimizing the distance between frozen and adapted branches (the list of numbers representing each node), while the topology-consistent loss ensures predictions respect graph structure via edge constraints.

paras: The core insight is this: the frozen branch preserves general knowledge learned from the big pre-training graphs—patterns about how graphs work that are true everywhere. The adapted branch learns the specific quirks of the new domain. Neither alone is enough. A frozen branch on a mismatched domain is blind to local differences; an adapted branch on a tiny dataset is unreliable, learning noise instead of signal.

By running both and pulling them into agreement via the contrastive loss, the model forces the adapters to learn differences that the pre-trained encoder will accept. In other words, the frozen branch acts as a judge: adapters can update, but only in ways that the old knowledge recognizes as sensible. The topology-consistent loss adds a second constraint: predictions must align with the graph's edge structure, so neighboring nodes push each other toward consistent answers.
When both constraints are satisfied, the final blend (averaging the two branches) is stable: it mixes proven old patterns with domain-specific updates, and both parts are internally coherent.

stages.s: Frozen branch reads graph (old knowledge fixed)
Adapted branch reads graph (new learning via adapters)
Contrastive loss: pull branches into agreement

math.words: total loss equals classification loss plus scaled contrastive loss plus scaled topology loss
math.equation: L_total = L_cls + lambda_1 * L_ctr + lambda_2 * L_fus
symbols: standard cross-entropy loss on labeled nodes
contrastive loss: penalizes distance between frozen and adapted representations
topology-consistent loss: ensures predicted labels respect graph edges
weight parameters controlling how much each loss contributes

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose on node A: L_cls = 0.5 (classification error), L_ctr = 0.2 (branches disagree), L_fus = 0.1 (edge conflict).
If adapters update to bring frozen and adapted closer, L_ctr drops to 0.1: L_total = 0.5 + 0.1 + 0.05 = 0.65, lower loss, training succeeds.
The contrastive term is the main lever: pulling the branches together is rewarded directly.

math.note: The three terms work as a single decision: optimize classification accuracy while forcing the two branches to stay aligned and respect graph structure.

charts.title: Frozen branch alone (old knowledge only)
charts.note: Locked knowledge cannot adapt; target domain suffers.

charts.title: Full fine-tuning (no old knowledge)
charts.note: Adapts to target but forgets source; no stable foundation.

charts.title: GP2F (both branches, aligned)
charts.note: Preserves old knowledge while adapting to new domain; both metrics strong.

items.b: Adapters overfit if the target dataset is too tiny.
items.html: If there are only a handful of labeled nodes, the adapters can memorize those few labels instead of learning general patterns, because with so few examples the model can fit them perfectly by accident. The contrastive loss helps by tying the adapters to the frozen branch, forcing them to stay sensible, but a frozen branch that is itself misaligned with the domain cannot fully rescue learning from extreme scarcity.

If the pre-trained encoder is wildly far from the target domain (e.g., pre-trained on social networks, deployed on molecules), the contrastive loss may struggle to pull the branches together, leaving them incoherent.

items.b: Graph structure is wrong or missing.
items.html: If the edges in the target graph are noisy or the topology does not reflect true relationships, the topology-consistent loss will enforce the wrong constraints, corrupting both branches.

When the source and target domains have enough structural similarity, adapters are lightly initialized to avoid disruption, and the contrastive and topology losses are balanced, the method yields a stable blend that inherits old knowledge and adapts smoothly.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small Python script that pre-trains a graph encoder on one graph (like Cora, a citation network), then loads a different small graph (like OGB-Arxiv, a paper-citation network) as the target. Create adapters and train GP2F for 10 epochs on 1-shot labels (one example per class). Track the accuracy on the frozen branch alone, the adapted branch alone, and the blended version. The blended version should beat both individual branches because the frozen branch is reliable and the adapted branch is fresh.
demo.closing: The core insight made visible: a single frozen model is stuck because it cannot adjust to new domains, a single adapted model is shaky because it overfits to tiny datasets, but two branches held in agreement are stronger than either alone because each stabilizes the other—the frozen branch anchors the adapters to sense, and the adapters ground the frozen branch to the target domain.
